# Chapter 1: Fast hands, slow hands

> **In one breath:** Agents write code much faster than you do, so stop competing with them at typing. Your job moves to everything *around* the code: the checks, the structure, the judgment. But mess still slows agents down, so the checks are not optional.

Insights: **I01 · I02 · I03**. Source concepts: C1, C2, C5 (see [SOURCES.md](../SOURCES.md)).

---

## Explain it like I'm five

Imagine a kitchen with a robot cook. The robot chops, stirs and fries ten times faster than the head chef. If the chef keeps grabbing the knife to "help", the whole kitchen goes at the chef's speed. So the smart chef puts the knife down.

But the robot is messy. It leaves peelings on the floor and dirty pans on every burner. After a while the kitchen gets so cluttered that even the robot starts dropping things, burning food and going in circles. So the chef's new job is to:

- write the recipe card (what to cook),
- set up the taste test (did it come out right?),
- put up a cleaning checklist (no dish leaves until the station is clean).

These checks slow the robot down a little. That's fine, as long as **robot + checks is still faster than the chef cooking alone.**

---

## The grown-up version

### I01 · Get the human out of the code loop

Uncle Bob (Robert C. Martin) describes the moment he started using coding agents seriously: they were fast, and having to read and fix their code made *him* the bottleneck. His conclusion, in his words: *"They are fast with code. I am slow with code."* So he hands the code to the agents and works on the scaffolding around it, aiming for a setup where he does not have to read the code at all.

Not reading the code does not mean not checking it. He swaps line-by-line review for other evidence: quality scores (CRAP, Chapter 3), spot checks, and test batteries the agents can't wriggle past.

### I02 · Mess compounds, for agents too

Messy code doesn't just look bad. It makes the next change harder, and that is as true for agents as for people. Uncle Bob saw agents get stuck in loops where fixing one thing broke another, spin without progress, and in one case say outright that they couldn't cope with the code any more. The level of mess that breaks an agent may differ from the level that breaks a human, but the cliff is real.

So "the agent wrote it, who cares what it looks like?" is a trap. Code quality is now a **performance input for your agents**, not just a courtesy to future humans.

### I03 · The productivity margin is the scoreboard

Every check you add slows the agents down. Add enough and they become slower than a human, at which point, as he puts it, you've lost the game. The quantity to watch is the **margin**: how much faster agents-plus-gates are than a competent human doing the same work.

He reports a margin of roughly **2x to 5x** with his full set of gates. For one story: a single unchecked agent pass takes minutes but gives questionable quality, his full multi-agent pipeline takes about an hour, and a human would take about half a day. Treat those numbers as his personal experience on his own projects, not a benchmark.

---

## Picture it

```
            BEFORE                                   AFTER
  +------------------------+          +---------------------------------+
  | human writes code      |          | agents write code (fast)        |
  | human reviews code     |  ---->   |   |                             |
  | human fixes code       |          |   v                             |
  | (everything at human   |          | gates check it (deterministic)  |
  |  speed)                |          |   |  fail -> agents fix, retry  |
  +------------------------+          |   v                             |
                                      | human: structure, judgment,     |
                                      |        spot checks, strategy    |
                                      +---------------------------------+

  margin = (human time for the task) / (agents + gates time)
           keep it > 1, or the gates have eaten your speed-up
```

---

## Why it matters to you

- **Your bottleneck moves.** If you review every line an agent writes, you've capped your throughput at your reading speed. That's the slow path the episode warns about.
- **Quality turns into speed.** A clean codebase is cheaper for agents to work in, so cleaning up is an investment in agent throughput, not overhead.
- **You need a number, not a feeling.** "Agents feel faster" isn't a margin. Time a few real tasks both ways.

## Try it this week

1. Pick one small feature. Time yourself doing it by hand (or estimate honestly).
2. Do it again with an agent and *your current* checks. Time it, including the time you spend reviewing and fixing.
3. Divide. That's your margin. Write it down and track it as you add gates in later chapters.
4. Watch the agent on a messy file and on a clean one. Do you see the "fix one, break another" thrash on the messy one?

## Watch out

- **"Don't read the code" is the end state, not step one.** Uncle Bob earned it by building gates first, and he still spot-checks. Skip the gates and you aren't delegating, you're just not looking.
- **Some code deserves human eyes anyway:** security boundaries, money movement, data deletion, anything regulated. The episode is about general application code. Use judgment.
- **The 2x-5x figure is anecdotal.** It's one expert's report. Your margin depends on your domain, your gates and your agents.

## Check yourself

Try to answer before opening each one.

<details><summary>1. Why is reviewing every line of agent output a problem, if you want speed?</summary>

Because then the whole system moves at human reading speed. The agents' speed advantage disappears into your review queue. The fix is to replace most reading with checks that run automatically.
</details>

<details><summary>2. "The agent wrote it, so code quality doesn't matter." What does the episode say?</summary>

Mess compounds for agents just like for humans. Past some level they thrash: they loop, break things while fixing others, and even give up. Clean code keeps agents productive.
</details>

<details><summary>3. You add five new quality checks, and now a feature takes your agents longer than it would take you. Who won?</summary>

Nobody. You've lost the game. The productivity margin (human time divided by agents-plus-gates time) has to stay above 1. Gates are worth it only while that's true.
</details>

# Chapter 2: Rules fade, gates don't

> **In one breath:** Long instruction files get obeyed loosely, because models attend to the start and end of their context and lose the middle. So keep the prompt short and move every *checkable* rule into a tool the agent must satisfy before it can stop.

Insights: **I04 · I05 · I06**. Source concepts: C3, C4, C24.

---

## Explain it like I'm five

Before a birthday party you tell a kid fifty rules. Later they remember the first one ("say hi to grandma") and the last one ("don't eat all the cake"). Rules 17 through 43 are gone.

Now picture a different trick. The playroom door has a lock that only opens when the toys are back in the box. Nobody has to remember the rule, because the door enforces it, every time, and doesn't get tired.

- A **rule** in the prompt is the fifty-item speech.
- A **gate** is the locked door.

You still say a few things up front ("we're going to grandma's, be kind"), but anything a machine can check, the machine checks.

---

## The grown-up version

### I04 · Steering decays

Uncle Bob's experience with long rule files (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` and friends): agents treat them, in his Pirates of the Caribbean joke, as *"more like guidelines."* He attributes this to the "lost in the middle" effect. Models give more weight to the beginning and end of their context than to the middle, so the 50th and 80th instructions in a long file effectively vanish.

Matt Pocock links this to Dex Horthy's "smart zone / dumb zone" framing: past a certain fill level, a context window gets measurably worse at following instructions.

This matches published research. Liu et al.'s *Lost in the Middle* (TACL 2024) found a U-shaped accuracy curve over position in context. Later work on instruction density found that compliance drops as you pile on simultaneous instructions. See [SOURCES.md](../SOURCES.md).

His response is to trim the initial prompt to the bare minimum, so that what's there sits in the high-attention zone, and then to enforce everything else with deterministic tools after the fact.

### I05 · The deterministic-tool loop

A **gate** is a command with a pass/fail exit code: a test suite, a complexity score, a dependency checker. The instruction to the agent turns from "please write clean code" into:

> Keep changing the code until this tool says it's okay.

The agent can't negotiate with an exit code, forget it in the middle of a long context, or decide it's "more of a guideline". Uncle Bob is open that this trades speed for quality, which is why Chapter 1's productivity margin matters: you pay for gates in agent time.

### I06 · The reading asymmetry

Matt Pocock pointed out that if you hand an agent a spec, it will read it. Uncle Bob added the mirror image: humans don't read what agents write. So:

| Audience | Length | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Written **for agents** (specs, role prompts, rule files) | Can be long *if needed*, though front-load what matters (I04) | Agents read everything they're given |
| Written **for humans** (summaries, PR descriptions, reports) | Must be short | Humans skim or skip agent output |

---

## Picture it

```
 attention
   ^
   |##                                                ##
   |###                                             ###
   |#####                                        #####
   |  ########                              ########
   |        ##############################
   +------------------------------------------------------>
    start        the middle of a long prompt          end
   (rule 1)     (rules 17..43 live here, and fade)   (rule 50)

  THE GATE LOOP
  +-------------+     +-------------------+   exit 0   +--------+
  | agent edits | --> | run gate commands | ---------> |  done  |
  |   the code  | <-- | (tests, crap,     |            +--------+
  +-------------+ fail|  fence, mutate)   |
                      +-------------------+
```

---

## Why it matters to you

- **Your 400-line `CLAUDE.md` is probably mostly ignored.** The rules that matter most should be few and at the top. The rest should become checks.
- **Gates compose; prompt rules compete.** Adding a tenth gate doesn't weaken the other nine. Adding a tenth prompt rule dilutes all of them.
- **It makes agents trustworthy in a specific, checkable way.** You don't have to trust the agent. You have to trust the gate, and you can test the gate (this repo tests its own).

## Try it this week

Sort every line of your agent instruction file into one of two buckets:

| Bucket | Example rule | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Checkable** | "Functions must be small and tested" | Turn it into a gate: `python tools/crap.py --threshold 6 src/` |
| **Checkable** | "Respect the layering" | Turn it into a gate: `python tools/fence.py fence.toml` |
| **Checkable** | "Write meaningful tests" | Turn it into a gate: `python tools/mutate.py --test "pytest -x" src/` |
| **Checkable** | "Use our formatting" | Turn it into a gate: your formatter/linter in check mode |
| **Generative** | "This is a payments service; correctness beats speed" | Keep it in the prompt, near the top |
| **Generative** | "Prefer small, reversible steps" | Keep it in the prompt, near the top |

Then use [`playbook/CLAUDE.md.template`](../playbook/CLAUDE.md.template) as a starting point: a short priority zone plus one line telling the agent which command must pass.

## Watch out

- **Not everything is checkable.** Taste, product judgment and naming are hard to gate, which is why a short prompt plus human strategic review (Chapter 8) still matter.
- **A gate is only as good as what it measures.** Coverage can be gamed by tests that assert nothing, which is exactly why mutation testing exists (Chapter 3). Ask "what would a lazy agent do to pass this?"
- **Gates can be too slow.** If one takes 20 minutes, agents sit idle and your margin collapses. Scope gates to changed files where you can (diff-scoped mutation testing, `--changed` modes).

## Check yourself

<details><summary>1. Why do rules in the middle of a long instruction file get ignored?</summary>

Models attend most to the beginning and end of their context (primacy and recency), so instructions in the middle get less weight. The research name is "lost in the middle".
</details>

<details><summary>2. What makes a gate different from a rule?</summary>

A gate is a deterministic tool with a pass/fail result, and the agent loops until it passes. It doesn't live in the context window, so it can't be diluted or forgotten. A rule is text the model may or may not weight heavily.
</details>

<details><summary>3. You're writing (a) a spec for an agent and (b) a summary of the agent's work for your manager. How should their lengths differ?</summary>

The spec can be as long as it needs to be, since agents read what they're sent (but front-load the important parts). The summary must be short, because humans don't read long agent output.
</details>

# Chapter 3: Boring tools come back

> **In one breath:** Two great quality techniques were shelved for decades because they were too tedious for people: the CRAP score and mutation testing. Agents don't get bored, so these old tools are now practical, and they make strong gates.

Insights: **I07 · I08 · I09**. Source concepts: C6, C7, C8. Hands-on: [`tools/crap.py`](../tools/crap.py), [`tools/mutate.py`](../tools/mutate.py).

---

## Explain it like I'm five

**CRAP score: "how scary is this function?"** Picture a maze. A maze with many twisty paths is harder than a straight hallway. Now turn the lights off in parts of it. Dark, twisty mazes are the scariest. In code:

- twisty = many `if`s and loops (**complexity**),
- lights on = tested (**coverage**).

A twisty function with no tests gets a huge score. A twisty function that's fully tested scores the same as its number of paths. A simple, tested function scores 1.

**Mutation testing: "does your proofreader actually read?"** A teacher wants to know if your proofreading buddy is any good, so she sneaks one typo into your essay and hands it over. If the buddy says "looks perfect!", the buddy isn't really checking. Mutation testing does this to your tests. It sneaks a tiny bug into your code (changes `<` to `<=`) and sees whether any test complains.

**Why now?** Both jobs are dull: thousands of tiny, repetitive checks. People hated doing them. Robots don't mind.

---

## The grown-up version

### I07 · The CRAP metric as a gate

**C.R.A.P.** (Change Risk Anti-Patterns) was created by Alberto Savoia and Bob Evans in 2007:

```
CRAP(f) = CC(f)^2 * (1 - coverage(f))^3 + CC(f)
```

- `CC` is cyclomatic complexity: 1 + the number of decision points (`if`, loops, `and`/`or`, `except`, ...).
- `coverage` is the fraction of the function's statements executed by tests.

Useful facts to remember:

| Situation | Score |
|---|---|
| Fully tested | exactly `CC` |
| Untested | `CC^2 + CC` (CC 2, untested, scores 6; CC 5, untested, scores 30) |
| CC above your threshold | can never pass, whatever the coverage, so you must split the function |

Uncle Bob says he tried CRAP around 2000 but set it aside because going through every function by hand took forever. Now he simply asks an agent to run CRAP over what it just did and clean up whatever scores badly. He reads the score the friendly way: a score of 6 means six pathways through the function, all covered by tests.

He has published his own CRAP tools for Java, Go and Clojure (`unclebob/crap4java`, `crap4go`, `crap4clj`). This repo's [`tools/crap.py`](../tools/crap.py) is an independent Python implementation of the same published formula.

### I08 · Mutation testing as the merciless hardener

How it works:

1. Make a **mutant**: copy the code with one small change (flip `<` to `<=`, `+` to `-`, `True` to `False`, `10` to `11`).
2. Run the whole test suite against it.
3. If a test fails, the mutant is **killed** (good). If everything passes, it **survived**, which proves that this behavior isn't pinned down by any assertion.
4. Write tests until every mutant dies.

Around 2000 a run like this took him all night. With agents and modern hardware he describes it taking about 30 minutes, with the agent plugging every hole it finds. In his pipeline the "hardener" agent does this job and is merciless about it.

**This repo has a worked example.** The first time `tools/mutate.py` ran on [`example/shop`](../example/shop), two mutants survived: `frozen=True` changed to `frozen=False` on two dataclasses. Every test still passed, because no test checked that receipts and line items can't be edited after creation. Two small tests fixed it (see `test_line_item_is_immutable` and `test_receipts_cannot_be_altered`). Coverage was already 100%, so coverage alone could never have caught this.

### I09 · Agents don't feel boredom, which unlocks shelved tools

The general lesson is a selection rule: **look for good ideas that were abandoned only because they were tedious.** Agents are fast, don't care how boring the work is, and do what they're told. Both CRAP and mutation testing fit: sound ideas killed purely by labor cost.

Some candidates of my own (not from the episode): exhaustive property-based tests, keeping docs in sync with code, full dependency upgrades with changelog review, and characterization tests for legacy code.

---

## Picture it

```
 CRAP for a function with CC = 4
   coverage:  0%    25%    50%    75%    100%
   score:    20.0  10.75   6.0   4.25    4.0
                          ^ exactly at a threshold of 6 = pass (gate fails only if > 6)

 MUTATION TESTING
   original:   if age >= 18: ...
   mutant #1:  if age >  18: ...   tests pass? -> SURVIVED  (nobody tested age == 18)
   mutant #2:  if age <  18: ...   tests fail  -> killed
   mutant #3:  if age >= 19: ...   tests pass? -> SURVIVED  (same hole)
   fix: add `assert is_adult(18)` and `assert not is_adult(17)`  -> all killed
```

---

## Why it matters to you

- **Coverage lies; mutation testing doesn't (as much).** 100% coverage only means the lines ran. Mutation testing checks that your assertions would notice a change.
- **CRAP gives agents a precise repair target.** "This function scores 14: split it or test the untested branches" is something an agent can act on. "Write cleaner code" isn't.
- **Cheap to adopt.** You already produce coverage, and CRAP is a tiny calculation on top of it.

## Try it this week

```bash
pip install pytest coverage
make crap      # CRAP report for tools/ and example/shop (fails if any function > 6)
make mutate    # mutation-test example/shop (fails if any mutant survives)
```

Then break something on purpose and watch the gate catch it:

1. Delete `test_shipping_is_free_at_exactly_fifty_dollars` from `example/tests/test_pricing.py`.
2. Run `make mutate`. Two mutants survive: `5000 -> 5001` and `>= -> >` in `pricing.py`. Coverage is still 100%, because the line still runs. What's gone is the only test that checks the exact $50.00 boundary.
3. Restore the test (`git checkout example/tests/test_pricing.py`). Everything dies again.

(Deleting the bulk-discount-at-ten test *won't* produce survivors, because two other tests also use exactly ten items. Mutation testing measures your suite as a whole, not individual tests.)

For your own language: Java (`crap4java`, PIT), Go (`crap4go`, gremlins), JS/TS (`js-crap-score`, Stryker), Rust (`cargo-crap`, `cargo-mutants`), Python (this repo's tools, `mutmut`, `cosmic-ray`).

## Watch out

- **100% mutation score is usually impossible.** Some mutants don't change behavior at all (**equivalent mutants**), and research estimates them at roughly 4-39% of mutants. You need a way to excuse them *with a written reason*. In `tools/mutate.py` that's a `# mutate: skip -- <reason>` comment.
- **Mutation testing is expensive** (mutants × test-suite time). Scope it to changed code, use incremental modes, and set a budget (`--max-mutants`).
- **CRAP's exponents were chosen by debate, not data**, as the authors themselves said. It's a useful heuristic, not a law of nature.
- **Assertion-free tests can pump coverage**, which can make CRAP look good. Pair CRAP with mutation testing. That's exactly why the episode's pipeline has both a cleaner and a hardener.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>1. A function has CC = 3 and no tests. What is its CRAP score? Does it pass a threshold of 6?</summary>

3² × (1 − 0)³ + 3 = 9 + 3 = **12**. It fails: 12 > 6.
</details>

<details><summary>2. A function has CC = 7 and 100% coverage. Can it pass a threshold of 6?</summary>

No. At full coverage CRAP equals CC, which is 7, and 7 > 6. The only fix is to reduce complexity, for example by splitting the function.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Your tests cover 100% of lines but a mutant survives. What does that tell you?</summary>

The line ran during tests, but no assertion depended on its exact behavior. Coverage measures execution, mutation testing measures detection. Write a test that fails on that exact change.
</details>

<details><summary>4. Why were these tools shelved in the first place, and why does that matter now?</summary>

They were too tedious and slow for humans, which is a labor-cost problem rather than a flaw in the idea. Agents don't get bored, so the cost that killed them is gone. Look for other ideas shelved for the same reason.
</details>

# Chapter 4: The relay race

> **In one breath:** Don't have one agent do everything in one long session. Run a relay of specialists (specifier, coder, cleaner, hardener, QA), each starting with a fresh context, doing one job, and handing off. A long session drifts in whatever direction it started.

Insights: **I10 · I11 · I12**. Source concepts: C9, C10, C11. Templates: [`playbook/roles/`](../playbook/roles/).

---

## Explain it like I'm five

A relay race has four runners. Each runs one leg as hard as they can and hands the baton on. Nobody runs the whole race, because by the end they'd be exhausted and slow.

Agents get "tired" too, in their own way. Their memory (the context window) fills up with everything that happened earlier, and the important bits get lost in the clutter. So each runner starts fresh, does one leg, and passes a clean baton (the finished work plus a short note).

There's a second problem. Imagine you and a friend are chatting about coffee, and someone walks by loudly describing a soap opera. Suddenly every coffee joke turns into a soap-opera joke. You can't un-hear it. That's what happens to an agent when one session gets steered somewhere: everything afterward follows that path. The only reliable fix is a fresh conversation.

---

## The grown-up version

### I10 · The five-seat relay

Uncle Bob's pipeline, in his description:

| Seat | Job | Its gate (what "done" means) |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Specifier** | Turns a human-written story into a **Gherkin** acceptance test (given / when / then) and a **QA procedure** written from a human user's point of view: "you are a person operating this system through the UI; prove it works." | Spec + QA procedure exist and are reviewable by a human |
| **2. Coder** | Writes unit tests and the code that implements the story, and makes the Gherkin pass | Tests + acceptance tests green |
| **3. Cleaner** | Runs CRAP analysis and general code review, and cleans up the mess the coder made (he expects there to be one) | CRAP under threshold, tests still green |
| **4. Hardener** | Runs mutation testing mercilessly and closes every hole; full coverage | No surviving mutants (minus documented equivalents) |
| **5. QA** | Turns the written QA procedure into an executable script that drives the system and gives a deterministic result | QA script passes |

He's candid about the cost: the handoffs add a lot of communication overhead. Even so, he reports the whole relay is still well ahead of a human (Chapter 1's margin).

Uncle Bob's public orchestrator, `unclebob/swarm-forge`, ships packs of roles along these lines: a two-role coder→cleaner pack, a four-role pack, and a six-role pack covering specification, implementation, cleanup, architecture, hardening and QA. Each agent works in its own git worktree, and work moves between them through committed handoffs.

### I11 · Born, do the task, die

Each agent is created for one task, does it, and exits, so the next one starts with a clean context. That keeps each context small and inside the high-attention zone (Chapter 2), and the lost-in-the-middle problem mostly goes away.

Trade-offs he names:

- **Cost:** startup is slow. An agent can take 10-15 seconds just to start, and then it has to rebuild its understanding of the codebase.
- **Benefit:** parallelism. Several coders can run at once on one laptop.

### I12 · A context window has momentum

Matt Pocock's observation: steer an agent one way early in a session and everything after follows that **trajectory**. The only way to clear it is to clear the context. Uncle Bob agreed and offered the coffee/soap-opera parable. The model can't separate the relevant thread from the noise that got mixed in.

Practical upshot: when an agent goes off the rails, **don't argue with it in the same session.** Fix the instructions and start a fresh one.

---

## Picture it

```
 human story
     |
     v
 [1 SPECIFIER] --Gherkin + QA procedure--> [2 CODER] --code + tests-->
                                                                     |
     +---------------------------------------------------------------+
     v
 [3 CLEANER: CRAP] --clean code--> [4 HARDENER: mutation] --hardened-->
                                                                     |
     +---------------------------------------------------------------+
     v
 [5 QA: executable script] --pass--> human looks at architecture, then next story

 each [box] = fresh agent: born -> does one job -> passes its gate -> dies
```

---

## Why it matters to you

- **Specialization beats one do-everything prompt.** Each role prompt is short and focused, so it stays in the smart zone.
- **Separation of duties catches errors.** The cleaner doesn't feel attached to the coder's mess, and the hardener assumes the tests are weak.
- **Fresh context is a debugging tool.** A drifting session costs more to rescue than to restart.

## Try it this week

1. Start with the two-seat version: **coder → cleaner**. Use [`playbook/roles/coder.md`](../playbook/roles/coder.md) and [`playbook/roles/cleaner.md`](../playbook/roles/cleaner.md).
2. Run each as a *separate* agent session. Pass work between them through git commits, not a shared chat.
3. When that works, add the **hardener** ([`hardener.md`](../playbook/roles/hardener.md)) with `make mutate` as its gate.
4. Finally, add the **specifier** and **QA** seats. See [`example/features/checkout.feature`](../example/features/checkout.feature) for a Gherkin spec that this repo actually executes as a test.

## Watch out

- **Overhead is real.** For a one-line fix, five agents is silly. Scale the relay to the risk of the change.
- **Handoff notes are a new failure point.** If the coder's note is vague, the cleaner starts confused. Keep handoffs structured: what changed, which gates pass, what's left.
- **Parallel coders need boundaries.** Two agents editing the same module will collide. The module structure in Chapter 5 is what makes parallelism safe.
- **"Fresh" doesn't mean "uninformed".** Each agent still needs the right short context: its role, the story, the gates. It just shouldn't carry yesterday's chatter.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>1. Name the five seats in order and the main gate for each.</summary>

Specifier (Gherkin + QA procedure), Coder (unit + acceptance tests green), Cleaner (CRAP), Hardener (mutation testing), QA (executable QA script passes).
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why not run all five roles in one long session?</summary>

The context fills up and gets lost in the middle, and early steering creates a trajectory that pollutes later work. Fresh, single-task agents keep context small and clean.
</details>

<details><summary>3. An agent has been steered into a bad approach. Should you keep correcting it in the same session?</summary>

Usually not. The trajectory persists, so it's better to fix the instructions and start a fresh session.
</details>

<details><summary>4. What's the cost of the born-do-die approach?</summary>

Startup time (seconds per agent, plus rebuilding its understanding of the codebase) and communication overhead between seats. He reports the relay is still much faster than a human.
</details>

---

# Chapter 5: Rooms with doors

> **In one breath:** Structure still matters, and for the same reason as with people: models understand compartmentalized code better. Ask the agents what the structure is, expect to be scared, design the modules yourself, and lock the design in with a dependency fence that a tool enforces.

Insights: **I13 · I14 · I15 · I16 · I17**. Source concepts: C12-C16. Hands-on: [`tools/fence.py`](../tools/fence.py), [`example/fence.toml`](../example/fence.toml).

---

## Explain it like I'm five

A good house has rooms, and each room has a job: you cook in the kitchen and sleep in the bedroom. Doors connect some rooms and not others. You can make a sandwich without knowing how the bathroom plumbing works.

A bad house is one giant room with the stove next to the bed and the bathtub in the hallway. Everyone (people *and* robots) gets confused about what goes where.

Now add **house rules**: "the kitchen opens to the dining room, never into the garage." Then post a guard at each door who checks every trip. That guard is the **dependency fence**.

Finally, think of a **TV remote**: a few simple buttons on the outside and lots of clever electronics inside. You use it without opening it. That's a **deep module**, and agents love them for the same reason you do.

---

## The grown-up version

### I13 · Interrogate the agents about structure, and expect to be scared

Uncle Bob's practice: ask the agents what the structure of the system is and how modules relate. He says the answers frightened him. Then he designs a module structure himself and gives the agents an implementation plan to get there.

He's tried to automate this design step and says it hasn't worked well so far. **Module design is still a human job** in his workflow.

### I14 · Have agents build your instruments

He had his agents build him an **architecture viewer**: a UML-style diagram of the modules and which way the dependencies run. He can click into a module to see its submodules and pull up the code. (His public repos include `uml-viewer`, which can overlay CRAP scores from `crap4clj`.)

The lesson generalizes: **agents are great at building the dashboards and tools you use to supervise agents.**

### I15 · The dependency fence

He describes another deterministic tool: a tight little specification file saying which module may depend on which and which way dependencies must flow. Agents can't violate it, because a checker runs at the end and fails the build.

When the fence fails, there are three standard repairs:

1. **Invert the dependency.** Make the low-level thing depend on the high-level one.
2. **Insert an interface.** Depend on an abstraction, not a concrete module.
3. **Split the module in half.** It was doing two jobs.

**In this repo:** [`example/fence.toml`](../example/fence.toml) says `checkout` may use `cart` and `pricing`, but **not** `storage`. Checkout still needs to load carts, so [`checkout.py`](../example/shop/checkout.py) declares a small `CartStore` interface and accepts any object that fits. That's repair #2 already applied. Run `make fence` to check it.

### I16 · Compartmentalization serves models like it serves humans

Uncle Bob's argument: well-partitioned code with disciplined interfaces is graspable by humans because we compartmentalize in our heads, and models do the same. Stuff a module with everything under the sun and the agent won't know what it's doing in there. It's the coffee/soap-opera problem from Chapter 4, at the scale of a module instead of a conversation.

### I17 · Deep modules are context economy

Matt Pocock brought in John Ousterhout's idea (*A Philosophy of Software Design*) that a **deep module** has a small, simple interface hiding a lot of implementation. He suggested this suits models well: they can read the interface and skip the implementation. Uncle Bob agreed. Agents pay attention to structure, and good structure lets them skip the code beneath, which he called both a danger and an advantage. It works as long as the code underneath is consistent. He added that agents also read **tests** to understand what a system does.

In context-window terms, a deep module is **cheap to load**: interface + doc comment + tests, without the internals.

---

## Picture it

```
 THE FENCE FOR example/shop          (arrows = "may import")

        +----------+
        | checkout |-------------+
        +----------+             |
          |      \               v
          |       \         +---------+
          |        +------->| pricing |
          v                 +---------+
     (CartStore                  |
      interface)                 v
          ^                 +---------+
          :  satisfies      |  cart   |  <- depends on nothing
     +---------+            +---------+
     | storage |------------------^
     +---------+

 checkout -> storage is FORBIDDEN. Checkout declares CartStore; storage happens to fit it.

 SHALLOW vs DEEP
   shallow:  [ big interface | tiny implementation ]     agent must read everything
   deep:     [ small iface ]
             [ ............. large hidden implementation ............. ]
             agent reads the iface + tests and moves on
```

---

## Why it matters to you

- **Structure is now a lever on agent performance**, not just maintainability. Messy boundaries mean confused agents and more thrash.
- **Architecture is enforceable.** A fence turns "please respect the layering" (a fading rule) into a failing build (a gate).
- **Your time is best spent here.** If agents write the code, the human's highest-leverage work is module boundaries and dependency direction.

## Try it this week

1. Ask your agent: *"Describe the module structure of this repo. Which modules depend on which? Where are the cycles?"* Compare the answer to what you believed.
2. Draw the dependency graph you *want*. Write it as a fence file. The format is in [`tools/fence.py`](../tools/fence.py).
3. Run the checker. Every violation is a design conversation: invert, interface, or split?
4. Add the fence to your gate command so no agent can merge a violation.
5. Ask an agent to build you a small viewer that renders the fence file and the actual imports as a diagram.

## Watch out

- **Deep modules have a danger side too,** which Uncle Bob flagged himself. If agents trust the interface and skip the implementation, an inconsistent implementation will mislead them. Mutation tests and contract tests keep interfaces honest.
- **A fence is only as good as its map.** If the map is wrong (modules carved along the wrong lines), enforcing it hard just makes the wrong structure rigid. Revisit it as the design evolves.
- **Don't let agents edit the fence to pass the gate.** Changing `fence.toml` is a *design* decision. Treat it like a code-owner-protected file.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>1. Your fence fails: module `billing` imports `email`, which isn't allowed. Name the three standard repairs.</summary>

Invert the dependency, insert an interface (for example, billing declares a `Notifier` interface that an email adapter implements), or split the module.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Why are deep modules especially good for agents?</summary>

The agent can understand and use them from the small interface (plus tests) without loading the large implementation. That saves context and attention.
</details>

<details><summary>3. In Uncle Bob's workflow, who designs the module structure: agents or humans?</summary>

Humans, for now. He interrogates the agents about the existing structure, designs the target structure himself, and gives them an implementation plan. His attempts to automate this haven't worked well yet.
</details>

---

# Chapter 6: Values, not rituals

> **In one breath:** Impose human *values* on agents (tested, clean, well-structured code) but not human *disciplines* (the exact rituals people use to get there). And thresholds may need to move: agents might handle more complexity per function than people can.

Insights: **I18 · I19**. Source concept: C17, C18.

---

## Explain it like I'm five

We want kids to have **clean teeth**. That's the value. To get there, we give kids a ritual: brush for two minutes, sing the song, top teeth then bottom teeth. The ritual exists because kids get bored, forget and rush.

Now imagine a robot that cleans teeth perfectly, but in its own order and without the song. Should we force it to sing? No. We should **check the teeth.** Keep the value and check the result. Let the ritual go if it was only there to help humans.

And the robot might be able to clean trickier teeth than a kid can, so the "this tooth is too hard to clean" line might sit in a different place for the robot.

---

## The grown-up version

### I18 · Values transfer, disciplines don't, thresholds move

This is the sharpest formulation in the conversation. Uncle Bob (paraphrased) thinks it's probably a mistake to impose a human *discipline* on an agent, but **not** a mistake to impose human *values*, though some thresholds may need to change.

Two concrete cases:

**1. TDD is a human discipline, so he doesn't enforce it on agents.**
This is notable coming from one of TDD's best-known advocates. He sees no sense in making an agent write one line of test, then one line of production code, back and forth. Agents naturally write a function and then its tests. He notes that this is closer to how John Ousterhout works (the two publicly debated TDD and function size in 2024-25), and since agents keep falling back to it, he accepts it. The **value** survives: everything is tested. The gates (coverage via CRAP, mutation testing) enforce the value without the ritual.

**2. CRAP thresholds move.**

| Who writes the code | His CRAP threshold |
|---|---|
| Humans | Keep it below ~4 |
| Agents | Set to 6, considering 8 |

His reasoning is that agents have a huge and perfectly accurate short-term memory, so they can hold more paths in mind than a human can. Treat that as **his working hypothesis**: I found no independent research confirming it. His own `crap4java` tool's README sets its failure line at 8.

### I19 · Agent debates generate hypotheses, not authority

He sometimes debates design questions with agents, such as what the CRAP threshold should be. He's explicit that you can't trust any debate you have with an agent, and he has them anyway. Use agent opinions to **generate ideas and surface arguments**, never as **evidence**. Agents are agreeable, persuadable, and confidently wrong in ways a measurement isn't.

---

## Picture it

```
              HUMANS                         AGENTS
 VALUE        tested, clean, structured  ==  tested, clean, structured   (same)
 DISCIPLINE   TDD red-green-refactor     !=  write fn, then its tests    (different ritual)
 THRESHOLD    CRAP <= ~4                 ->  CRAP <= 6 (maybe 8)         (moves)
 ENFORCED BY  habit, review, pairing     ->  deterministic gates         (different mechanism)
```

---

## Why it matters to you

- **Stop copying human process onto agents by default.** Ask of each practice: "Is this the value, or a ritual that helps humans reach the value?"
- **Measure outcomes, not process.** You can't watch an agent "do TDD" meaningfully, but you can measure coverage and mutation score.
- **Tune your thresholds with evidence.** Run your gates at 6 for a while, then 8, and watch the thrash rate and defect rate. Don't settle it by asking the agent.

## Try it this week

Make a three-column table for your team's practices:

| Practice | The value behind it | How a gate could check the value |
|---|---|---|
| TDD | Every behavior is tested | Coverage + mutation score |
| Small functions | Code is understandable and changeable | CRAP threshold |
| Code review | Defects and design flaws get caught | Gates + human architecture review + spot checks |
| "Clean architecture" | Dependencies point toward policy | Dependency fence |

For any practice where the right column is empty, either invent a gate or keep it as a human responsibility on purpose.

## Watch out

- **Some disciplines carry values you haven't named.** Code review also spreads knowledge across the team. If agents write the code and nobody reads it, where does that knowledge come from? (Chapter 8 tackles this.)
- **A looser threshold is an experiment, not a conclusion.** He's still deciding between 6 and 8 himself.
- **Don't swap "the agent agrees" for evidence.** That includes asking an agent whether this chapter is right.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>1. Distinguish a value from a discipline using TDD as the example.</summary>

Value: every behavior is covered by tests that would catch regressions. Discipline: the specific red-green-refactor micro-cycle humans use to get there. Uncle Bob enforces the value on agents (through gates) but not the discipline.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What CRAP thresholds does he use for humans vs agents, and why the difference?</summary>

Below ~4 for humans; 6 (maybe 8) for agents. He attributes the difference to agents' large, accurate short-term memory. That's his hypothesis, not established research.
</details>

<details><summary>3. You ask an agent "Should our threshold be 6 or 8?" and it argues convincingly for 8. Now what?</summary>

Treat it as a hypothesis worth testing. Run with 8 and measure thrash, defects and margin. An agent debate is not evidence.
</details>

---

# Chapter 7: The one-dollar house

> **In one breath:** When change is nearly free, giant up-front plans lose their point, because they're the old waterfall temptation in new clothes. Work in small batches, look at the result, adjust. The finished system is the real specification. And to specify a tool, point your agents at a good example rather than writing a long description.

Insights: **I20 · I21 · I22 · I23 · I24**. Source concepts: C19-C23.

---

## Explain it like I'm five

You're building a Lego house. If every brick cost $1,000 and took a week to place, you'd draw careful blueprints first. Mistakes would be expensive.

Now imagine every change costs **one dollar** and takes a second. Would you spend a month on blueprints? No. You'd build a bit, look at it, move the door, add a window, look again. The house itself shows you what you want.

Also, when you want a treehouse like your friend's, you don't write a 20-page description. You **point**: "Like that one, but for my tree, and with a rope ladder."

---

## The grown-up version

### I20 · Heavy up-front specs are the 1970s temptation, replayed

Uncle Bob sees an old pattern returning: the urge to specify, specify, specify, then hand everything to the agent. In the 70s the same urge gave us the **waterfall** process.

He was trying exactly this the week of the conversation and says it keeps going wrong. You write a big plan, the agents start, and partway through you discover they can't follow it because the plan didn't anticipate everything. They charge off in a bad direction, and you have to stop, back up and rewrite the plan. He also notes that agents *love* writing plans. The plans look beautiful and fall apart at the end.

On **spec-driven development** (a popular 2025-26 approach), his impression is that it probably won't work. This is one of the clearest points where the conversation pushes back on current fashion.

### I21 · Agile small batches, for agents

His alternative: let the agents do a story or two, look at the architecture, maybe intervene by hand, then a few more stories. He admits we may never escape that manual "organize the structure" step at the end of each batch, though he's trying.

### I22 · The $1 house: when change is cheap, plan less

His thought experiment: if every change to a house cost $1, nobody would pay an architect for a perfect up-front design. You'd fiddle until it looked right. He argues that agents have pushed the cost of code changes about as close to zero as we'll ever get, so the case for expensive up-front planning collapses.

### I23 · Specs are ephemeral; the end result is the specification

In his workflow the specs (stories, Gherkin, plans) are **ephemeral**: used, then gone. He points out that source code used to be the final specification, the one thing humans wrote and kept, and that role no longer exists in the same way. Instead of writing a spec that defines what he wants, he looks at the end result and treats *that* as the specification.

Matt Pocock asked whether *persistence* is what separates spec-driven development from this, meaning spec-driven development keeps the spec around. Uncle Bob's answer: his specs don't persist.

### I24 · Point, don't download

He has published his CRAP tools, mutation tester and agent harness, and his advice is surprising: **don't download them.** He wrote them for himself. Instead, point your agents at them, have the agents study them, and build your own version. He sees this as a far better way to specify the *essence* of a tool and customize it to your situation.

**This repo follows that advice.** The Python tools in [`tools/`](../tools/) were written independently from the published formulas and descriptions, not ported from his code, and they're single-file and dependency-free so your agent can read one and build its own.

---

## Picture it

```
 WATERFALL (expensive change)            ONE-DOLLAR HOUSE (cheap change)
 spec spec spec spec spec                story -> build -> LOOK
            |                                 ^              |
            v                                 |   adjust     |
          build build build                   +--------------+
            |                            every 1-2 stories: human reviews architecture
            v
        "it doesn't match"               spec = the thing you can see working

 POINT, DON'T DOWNLOAD
   "Here is tools/crap.py. Study it. Build one for our TypeScript monorepo
    that reads istanbul JSON, gates at 6, and checks only changed files."
```

---

## Why it matters to you

- **Beware the beautiful agent plan.** A plan that looks thorough isn't proof that the agents can execute it. Prefer a thin slice that works.
- **Small batches are a structural safety valve.** Reviewing architecture every story or two catches drift while it's cheap to fix.
- **Exemplars beat descriptions.** One good example file teaches an agent more than pages of requirements.

## Try it this week

1. Next feature: instead of a big plan, write **one** story. Let the agent build it through your gates. Look at the result, then write the next story.
2. After every one or two stories, spend 10 minutes on the architecture: run `make fence`, look at the CRAP report, ask the agent to describe the structure.
3. Pick one tool from this repo. Point your agent at it and ask it to build the equivalent for your stack. Compare the two.

## Watch out

- **"No big plan" is not "no thinking".** The human still owns strategy, module boundaries and what to build. The batch is small; the intent isn't vague.
- **Not every domain has $1 changes.** Database migrations, public APIs, hardware, regulated systems and anything with external users carry real change costs. Plan more where change is expensive.
- **Ephemeral specs can cost you the "why".** If specs vanish, record important decisions somewhere durable (ADRs, commit messages), or the reasoning goes with them.
- **This is one practitioner's view on spec-driven development.** Teams report success with spec-first workflows too. Test it in your context; both views are hypotheses.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>1. Why does Uncle Bob compare heavy agent specs to waterfall?</summary>

Both rest on the idea that you can specify everything up front. In practice the agents hit cases the plan didn't anticipate, go off course, and force you to back up and re-plan, just as waterfall projects discovered problems late.
</details>

<details><summary>2. What is the "$1 house" argument in one sentence?</summary>

When every change is nearly free, the expensive up-front design that exists to avoid costly changes stops paying for itself, so you iterate instead.
</details>

<details><summary>3. He published his tools. What does he tell you to do with them, and why?</summary>

Don't download them. Point your agents at them so they can study them and build versions tailored to you. An exemplar specifies the essence of a tool better than a description.
</details>

---

# Chapter 8: The general and the sergeant

> **In one breath:** Agents are excellent tacticians and poor strategists, so the human job is strategy. But you can only supervise work you understand, so the next generation still needs to learn to code: first by hand, then as an "agent" under the same gates, then running agents. And the old fundamentals keep coming back, because they're about organizing complexity, which models need too.

Insights: **I25 · I26 · I27 · I28**. Source concepts: C25-C28.

---

## Explain it like I'm five

In an army, the **sergeant** knows how to get the squad across the river: who carries what, where to step. The **general** decides *which* river to cross, and whether to cross at all. Agents are amazing sergeants and terrible generals.

To become a good general, though, you need to have waded a few rivers yourself. A swimming coach can tell a swimmer who is *playing* from one who is *drowning*, because the coach has struggled in the water. Someone who's never swum can't tell the difference.

And every time a new tool arrives, people panic that the old rules are dead. Then, a year later, they're picking the old rules up off the floor, dusting them off, and remembering why they needed them.

---

## The grown-up version

### I25 · Tactical vs strategic: agents took the sergeant's job

Matt Pocock raised Ousterhout's distinction between **tactical** programming (get this feature working now) and **strategic** programming (invest in design so the whole system stays easy to change). Uncle Bob agreed with the sergeant/general framing: agents are really good at tactics and really bad at strategy. Both reached for their copies of Ousterhout's book during this part of the conversation.

### I26 · Human as subagent: the education gauntlet

How should a new engineer learn when agents write the code? Uncle Bob's proposed path:

1. **Write code yourself for about a year**, so you know what the agents are dealing with.
2. **At a company, be treated as an agent.** The lead engineer gives you the same kinds of tasks the agents get and runs you through the same deterministic tools. You spend several months being, in his words, horribly unproductive while learning a huge amount.
3. **Then you may be trusted to run an agent yourself**, under supervision at first.

Underneath that he describes a learning ladder: binary, assembly language, a language like C, a higher-level language like Python, and finally strategically running an agent under supervision. His argument for the low rungs: if all you ever do is write Java, you live in a fantasy world. You don't know what's really happening under the abstraction.

Matt Pocock added a hopeful note: agents compress feedback loops. Strategic mistakes that used to take nine months to show up can now show up fast enough to learn from. His half-joke: become the agent, and have the agent delegate to you.

### I27 · Recognizing thrash is the key diagnostic skill

How did Uncle Bob know the agents were failing when he first used them seriously? He watched them **thrash**, and he recognized the struggle because he had been through it himself. A novice would come in and not recognize it.

His cure for the novice: **read the old books.** He names Tom DeMarco, Ed Yourdon and *The Pragmatic Programmer*, and suggests filtering out the dated parts. Those books were written in the 70s and 80s, when these lessons were first learned.

### I28 · Fundamentals persist up every abstraction rung

His closing argument: software may be the most complex thing humans attempt. (He attributed a version of that line to Dijkstra; I couldn't verify the exact quote.) The fundamentals are how we organize that complexity into something that can be understood, not just by humans but by models, which are modeled on humans.

History rhymes. Binary to assembly, assembly to compilers, compilers to models: every step brought the same panic that the old rules were dead. His warning, roughly: **the rules you throw away now are the ones you'll be picking up off the floor in a year, remembering why you needed them.** He closed by holding up the second edition of *Clean Code* (2025).

---

## Picture it

```
 WHO DOES WHAT
   strategic (the general):  which problem? which modules? which direction?  -> HUMAN
   tactical  (the sergeant): implement, test, refactor, harden               -> AGENTS

 THE EDUCATION GAUNTLET
   [learn the stack: binary -> assembly -> C -> Python]
          |
   [~1 year writing code by hand]
          |
   [months as a "human subagent": same tasks, same gates as the agents]
          |
   [run an agent under supervision]
          |
   [run agents strategically]

 THE ABSTRACTION LADDER (same panic at every rung; fundamentals survive)
   binary -> assembly -> compilers -> high-level languages -> models
```

---

## Why it matters to you

- **Your durable value is judgment:** choosing problems, shaping modules, spotting thrash, deciding direction.
- **Diagnosis needs experience.** If you've never written the kind of code your agents write, you can't tell productive work from flailing. Keep your hands in.
- **Fundamentals are the operating manual for agents.** Coupling, cohesion, information hiding and testing aren't legacy concerns. They're how you make a codebase agent-friendly (Chapters 2 and 5).

## Try it this week

1. **Thrash spotting:** watch an agent session on a hard task without intervening. Note the moments it loops, reverts itself, or "fixes" one test by breaking another. What structural problem was underneath?
2. **Be the subagent:** take one ticket your agents usually get, do it by hand, and run it through `make check`. How did the gates feel from the inside?
3. **Old books:** pick one, such as *The Pragmatic Programmer*, DeMarco's *Structured Analysis*, Yourdon & Constantine's *Structured Design*, Parnas's 1972 paper on decomposing systems into modules, or Brooks's *The Mythical Man-Month*. Read one chapter and ask: "How does this apply to agents?"

## Watch out

- **The gauntlet is a proposal, not a proven program.** Nobody has run this apprenticeship at scale yet. It's a thoughtful hypothesis from an experienced practitioner.
- **"Learn assembly first" is contested.** Plenty of strong engineers never wrote assembly. The underlying point (understand at least one layer below your abstraction) is broadly accepted; the specific ladder is his preference.
- **Strategy isn't safe forever.** Agents' strategic ability may improve. The episode describes the state of things in mid-2026.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>1. In the sergeant/general framing, which role do agents play and which do humans keep?</summary>

Agents are the sergeants: tactical execution. Humans are the generals: strategic choices about direction, structure and trade-offs.
</details>

<details><summary>2. Describe the "human as subagent" stage and why it exists.</summary>

A junior engineer receives the same tasks agents get and goes through the same deterministic gates, under a lead. It builds the hands-on understanding needed later to supervise agents and to recognize their thrash.
</details>

<details><summary>3. Why can an experienced engineer spot agent thrash that a novice misses?</summary>

They've been through the same struggle themselves, so they recognize the pattern: looping, breaking one thing while fixing another, spinning on tangled code.
</details>

<details><summary>4. Why do fundamentals still matter if models write the code?</summary>

Fundamentals organize complexity into understandable pieces, and models, being modeled on humans, benefit from the same organization. Every abstraction jump has triggered a "the old rules are dead" panic, and the rules came back.
</details>

# Cheat sheet: Uncle Bob on software fundamentals in the age of AI

**The whole episode in one sentence:** let agents write the code, but build a cage of deterministic checks and good structure around them, because the fundamentals that make code manageable for humans make it manageable for models.

## The 28 insights in one line each

**1 · Fast hands, slow hands**
- **I01** Agents are fast at code, you're slow: give them the code and take the scaffolding.
- **I02** Mess compounds for agents too; past a point they thrash and give up.
- **I03** Score yourself on the margin: agents + gates must beat a human (he reports 2-5x).

**2 · Rules fade, gates don't**
- **I04** Long prompt rules become "guidelines" (lost in the middle). Keep the prompt tiny.
- **I05** Gate loop: change the code until the tool says OK.
- **I06** Agents read everything; humans read nothing agents write. Long for agents, short for humans.

**3 · Boring tools come back**
- **I07** CRAP = CC² × (1 − cov)³ + CC. Fully tested gives CRAP = CC.
- **I08** Mutation testing: inject tiny bugs; every mutant must make a test fail.
- **I09** Revive ideas that died only of tedium. Agents don't get bored.

**4 · The relay race**
- **I10** Specifier → Coder → Cleaner (CRAP) → Hardener (mutation) → QA (script).
- **I11** Agents are born, do one task, and die. Fresh context, parallel coders, slow startup.
- **I12** Sessions have momentum; reset the context to reset the trajectory.

**5 · Rooms with doors**
- **I13** Ask agents about the structure, get scared, design the modules yourself.
- **I14** Have agents build your instruments (an architecture viewer).
- **I15** Dependency fence: a spec file plus a checker. Repairs: invert, interface, split.
- **I16** Compartments help models like they help humans.
- **I17** Deep modules mean agents read the interface and tests, not the internals.

**6 · Values, not rituals**
- **I18** Impose values (tested, clean), not disciplines (strict TDD). Thresholds move: CRAP ~4 for humans, 6-8 for agents.
- **I19** Debating with agents gives you hypotheses, not evidence.

**7 · The one-dollar house**
- **I20** Big up-front agent specs = waterfall again. Beautiful plans fall apart.
- **I21** Small batches: a story or two, then look at the architecture.
- **I22** Change costs about $1 now, so fiddle until it's right instead of over-planning.
- **I23** Specs are ephemeral; the working result is the spec.
- **I24** Point, don't download: agents study an exemplar and build your version.

**8 · The general and the sergeant**
- **I25** Agents are tactical sergeants; humans are strategic generals.
- **I26** Learning path: code by hand ~1 year, then be a "human subagent" under the gates, then run agents.
- **I27** Spotting thrash takes having struggled. Read the old books.
- **I28** Fundamentals survive every abstraction jump. Thrown-away rules come back.

## Numbers worth remembering

| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| CRAP threshold for human code (his) | below ~4 |
| CRAP threshold for agent code (his) | 6, maybe 8 |
| Classic CRAP "crappy" line (Savoia & Evans) | 30 |
| CC 2, untested | CRAP 6 |
| CC 5, untested | CRAP 30 |
| Agent startup cost he cites | ~10-15 s |
| Mutation run, ~2000 vs now (his account) | overnight vs ~30 min |
| Margin he reports | ~2x-5x |
| Equivalent mutants (research) | ~4-39% of mutants |

## The loop, drawn

```
 story -> [specifier] -> [coder] -> [cleaner: CRAP] -> [hardener: mutation] -> [QA script]
              each seat: fresh agent, one job, must pass its gate, then exits
 every 1-2 stories: human reviews architecture (fence, viewer, CRAP report)
```

## This repo's gates

```bash
make crap     # fails if any function's CRAP > 6
make mutate   # fails if any mutant survives
make fence    # fails if a module imports something it isn't allowed to
make check    # all of the above, plus tests and generated-file freshness
```

---

# Critical lens: agreements, tensions and counterpoints

Understanding an argument includes knowing where it's strong, where it's contested, and what it leaves out. This page separates three things that are easy to blur:

1. **Where the two speakers agree** (from the episode)
2. **Where the conversation pushes against itself or against current fashion** (from the episode)
3. **Counterpoints and gaps** (from outside the episode: my analysis and published research, labeled as such)

---

## 1. Where Matt Pocock and Uncle Bob agree

| Topic | Who proposed it | The other's response |
|---|---|---|
| Deep modules are good for models (I17) | Pocock, via Ousterhout | Bob: agrees, adding that it's "both a danger and an advantage" |
| Agents are tactical, not strategic (I25) | Pocock, via Ousterhout | Bob: agrees; both pull out their copies of Ousterhout's book |
| Sessions have trajectory; clear the context to reset (I12) | Pocock | Bob: agrees and adds the coffee/soap-opera parable |
| Long steering degrades (smart zone / dumb zone) (I04) | Bob (lost in the middle) | Pocock: connects it to Dex Horthy's framing |
| Agents read what they're given; humans don't read agent output (I06) | Pocock | Bob: adds the mirror half |
| Feedback loops for learning strategy are faster now (I26) | Pocock | Bob's apprenticeship model rests on the same idea |

The overall picture is a **host who brings modern agent-engineering vocabulary** (Ousterhout, Horthy, trajectory) and a **guest who maps it onto fifty years of practice**. They agree more than they disagree.

## 2. Tensions inside the conversation

These are the most interesting places to think hard.

**a) The TDD champion doesn't impose TDD on agents (I18).**
Uncle Bob is one of TDD's best-known advocates, and he publicly debated Ousterhout on it in 2024-25. Here he lets agents write code first and tests after, which is closer to Ousterhout's style. His reconciliation is that TDD is a human discipline serving a value (everything tested), and gates enforce the value. *Question to sit with:* was TDD ever only about test coverage, or also about design pressure (writing the test first shapes the interface)? If it's the latter, what gives agents that pressure? His candidates would be the CRAP gate and the fence.

**b) "Don't read the code" vs "you must have written code to supervise" (I01 vs I26-I27).**
He aims to never read agent code, yet his ability to spot thrash comes from decades of reading and writing code. His apprenticeship model is his answer to this tension: he wants humans to build that experience deliberately, under the gates. It's still an open question whether that produces the same depth of judgment.

**c) Spec-driven development (I20, I23).**
Pocock raises spec-driven development, a popular approach in 2025-26. Uncle Bob is skeptical: he expects heavy specs to repeat waterfall, and his own specs are ephemeral. This is the episode's clearest disagreement with current fashion. Note that it's a prediction, and teams do report success with spec-first agent workflows.

**d) Automating architecture.**
Bob says the human still designs module structure (I13) and that his attempts to automate it haven't worked (I21). The whole system depends on a step that doesn't yet scale beyond the human.

## 3. Counterpoints and gaps (outside the episode)

These are **my analysis, informed by published research**, not claims made in the episode.

**Gates measure what's measurable.** CRAP, mutation testing and a dependency fence say nothing about:
- **security** (injection, auth bypass, secrets): you need SAST, dependency scanning and threat modeling;
- **performance**: you need benchmarks and budgets;
- **UX and product fit**: the QA seat covers flows, not whether users want it;
- **data correctness at scale**, migrations, privacy compliance.

A "never read the code" stance should be scoped to what your gates cover. For high-stakes paths, human review still pays for itself.

**Metric gaming is the classic failure of metric gates.** Agents optimize what you measure (Goodhart's law). Known holes:
- assertion-free tests inflate coverage and so lower CRAP (mutation testing plugs this, which is why both gates matter);
- splitting functions mechanically lowers CC without improving design (Ousterhout's "shallow modules" warning);
- agents may write tests that pin the *current* behavior, bugs included.

**100% mutation score is generally unreachable.** Equivalent mutants (changes that don't alter behavior) are undecidable to detect in general, and studies estimate them at roughly 4-39% of mutants. A "merciless" hardener needs a documented way to excuse them, or it will either loop forever or "kill" them with absurd tests. (`tools/mutate.py` uses a `# mutate: skip -- <reason>` comment.)

**CRAP's exponents were set by discussion, not calibration.** Its authors said so. It's a good heuristic for "complex and untested", not a precise risk measure. It's also blind to coupling between functions.

**Several numbers are one person's experience.** The 2x-5x margin, the 30-minute mutation runs and the "perfect short-term memory" rationale come from one expert on his own (often Clojure) projects. They're plausible and worth testing, not established.

**The relay has coordination costs.** Brooks's law ("adding manpower to a late project makes it later") has an agent analogue: more agents means more handoffs. Bob acknowledges the overhead; small tasks may not justify five seats.

**Who tests the tester?** If gates are the only check, the gates themselves must be correct. A buggy CRAP tool or a fence with a wrong map silently waves bad code through. (That's why this repository tests its tools, and the tools pass their own gates.)

**Team and legacy context.** The episode reflects a solo expert's workflow. In teams, the fence file and thresholds become shared agreements. On legacy codebases, an immediate hard gate can block all work, so ratchets (no function may get worse) are the usual on-ramp.

## Open questions worth tracking

1. Can module design (the strategic step) be automated, or will it stay human?
2. What's the right CRAP threshold for agent-written code: 6, 8, or something that depends on the model?
3. Does the "human subagent" apprenticeship produce engineers with strong judgment?
4. Do ephemeral specs lose institutional memory ("why is it like this?") over years?
5. As models improve, which of today's gates become unnecessary, and which become *more* important?

# Sources, provenance and confidence

This file explains where every claim in this repository comes from and how much weight it can bear. Please read it before you quote anything from here.

## The episode

| | |
|---|---|
| **Title** | LIVE: Uncle Bob on Software Fundamentals in the Age of AI |
| **URL** | https://www.youtube.com/live/zcLPGC-tvgk |
| **Host** | Matt Pocock |
| **Guest** | Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob") |
| **Date** | Wednesday, 19 August 2026 (livestream) |
| **Length** | about 57 minutes |
| **Format** | Two-person video conversation; no slides or screen shares reported |

## How this repository was built, and its limits

**I could not watch the video directly.** The environment that produced this repository had no network access to YouTube. Instead, the insights were reconstructed from secondary sources and cross-checked against each other:

1. **The primary secondary source** is a community analysis of the episode built from the video's own auto-captions: the *Concept Ledger* and *Extraction* notes in [Island-Dev-Crew/uncle-bob-skills](https://github.com/Island-Dev-Crew/uncle-bob-skills) (`docs/01-CONCEPT-LEDGER.md`, `docs/00-EXTRACTION.md`). It breaks the conversation into 28 numbered concepts (**C1-C28**), each backed by a short quote from the auto-captions. The `C` numbers in this repo refer to that ledger, so you can trace any insight back to its quote there.
2. **Independent corroboration** came from search-engine summaries of other write-ups of the same episode, which agree on the core claims: the five-role agent pipeline (specifier, coder, cleaner, hardener, QA), reviving CRAP and mutation testing as agent-run gates, deterministic gates over prompt steering, and "values, not disciplines":
   - besthub.dev, *Uncle Bob's AI Coding Pipeline: 5-Agent Gauntlet & Architecture Governance* (26 Aug 2026)
   - sozai.app transcript summary: https://sozai.app/transcript/uncle-bob-software-fundamentals-ai/
   - howardism.dev articles on Robert C. Martin and reviving impractical quality tools
   - daily.dev listing: https://daily.dev/posts/live-uncle-bob-on-software-fundamentals-in-the-age-of-ai-tb2uozdzr
   - Matt Pocock's announcement posts on X ("If your code sucks, your agent will too...")
3. **Primary artifacts I checked directly:** the READMEs of Uncle Bob's public repositories [`unclebob/crap4java`](https://github.com/unclebob/crap4java), [`unclebob/crap4go`](https://github.com/unclebob/crap4go), [`unclebob/crap4clj`](https://github.com/unclebob/crap4clj) and [`unclebob/swarm-forge`](https://github.com/unclebob/swarm-forge). They exist, implement the CRAP formula quoted in Chapter 3, and (for swarm-forge) describe two-, four- and six-role agent packs.

What this means for you:

- The **ideas and their attribution** are well supported: several independent sources agree.
- The **exact wording** of the short quotes comes from auto-captions as recorded by the community ledger. Auto-captions garble words: the ledger notes, for example, "claw.md" for CLAUDE.md, "Dex Hardy" for Dex Horthy and "crap" for C.R.A.P. Treat the quotes as close to verbatim, not as certified transcripts.
- **Speaker attribution** (who said what) follows the ledger's reading of a two-voice conversation and is occasionally a judgment call.
- If precision matters (for a talk, an article, a decision), **watch the relevant part of the video yourself.** The ledger's concept numbers make each claim easy to find.

| `episode+verified` | Said in the episode, and the factual part was checked independently (see below) |
| `episode+anecdotal` | Said in the episode, but it's the speaker's personal experience or hypothesis (numbers, rationales), with no independent evidence found |

## Factual claims checked independently

| Uncle Bob publishes CRAP tools and an agent orchestrator | Verified | `unclebob/crap4java`, `crap4go`, `crap4clj`, `swarm-forge` |
| "Lost in the middle": LLMs use the start and end of long contexts better than the middle | Verified | Liu et al., *Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts*, TACL 2024 |
| "Smart zone / dumb zone" framing is Dex Horthy's (HumanLayer) | Verified per the community research notes; the caption reads "Dex Hardy" | Horthy, *12-Factor Agents*; Pragmatic Engineer interview |
| Mutation testing dates to Lipton (1971) and DeMillo, Lipton & Sayward (1978) | Verified | DeMillo, Lipton & Sayward, "Hints on Test Data Selection", *IEEE Computer*, 1978 |
| A 100% mutation score is generally unreachable because of equivalent mutants | Verified (research consensus) | Budd & Angluin (1982) on undecidability; empirical studies estimate roughly 4-39% equivalent mutants |

| "Software is the most complicated thing humans have attempted" attributed to Dijkstra | **Not verified as a verbatim Dijkstra quote**; he hedged it himself | nearest: Dijkstra, *The Humble Programmer* (EWD340) |
